A1.justification: Both PDFs describe KGGen and the MINE benchmark. All 16 pages of v1 and 24 pages of v2, including figures, tables, appendices, and the added checklist, are readable. Retained experiments and illustrations can be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original MINE evaluations of KGGen, GraphRAG, and OpenIE, including quantitative scores and extracted-graph examples in Figures 3–5.

after.justification: v2 retains the original results and adds retrieval, human-annotated entity extraction, model comparisons, manual validation, and scaling/cost experiments.

M1.justification: v1 Section 3.3 uses repeated full-list LLM clustering, cluster validation, and subsequent batch reassignment. v2 Section 4.3 replaces this with S-BERT/k-means grouping, BM25/embedding candidate retrieval, and LLM duplicate identification with canonical aliases. Appendix A also revises extraction constraints and replaces the clustering/validation prompts with a duplicate-resolution prompt.

E1.justification: The original synthetic-article MINE task remains as MINE-1. v2 adds WikiQA-based retrieval over an aggregated Wikipedia corpus, entity extraction on human-annotated SemEval-2010 Task 8 sentences, and extraction/scaling experiments using The Name of the Wind. These expand both represented text sources and task requirements.

E2.justification: OpenIE and GraphRAG remain the competing extractors in the matched MINE/MINE-1 comparison. The added retrieval and scaling experiments use the existing GraphRAG comparator; OpenIE remains in MINE-1 but is excluded from the new MINE-2 task because it lacks source-chunk links. Cross-model tests evaluate KGGen variants.

E3.justification: v2 introduces hybrid retrieval of 10 triples plus 10 two-hop triples, source-text-assisted answering, and answer judging for MINE-2. It adds manual-validation sampling and a 100-sentence SemEval protocol with markup removal and flexible entity matching. The described extraction backend changes from GPT-4o to Gemini 2.0 Flash. MINE article length is revised from approximately 1,000 words to a mean of 592; this does not establish that the corpus was regenerated.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained qualitative graph examples, v2 adds sensitivity to the underlying LLM, a human audit of 60 fact–graph judgments, manual validity assessment of 100 triples per extractor, and analyses of relation reuse, de-duplication, and computational scaling. These test reliability and practical behavior that v1 did not investigate.

E5.justification: v2 adds error bars to the MINE-2 comparison in Figure 5, whereas v1 reports across-article score distributions without such bars. Their meaning and calculation are not specified, and neither version provides experimental seed or repeated-run counts. The checklist's assertion of error-bar reporting supplies no further statistical definition.

E6.justification: The original MINE scores remain 66.07% for KGGen, 47.80% for GraphRAG, and 29.84% for OpenIE. Added results include MINE-2 scores of 80.63% versus 81.20%, SemEval extraction success of 96/100, and Table 1's model scores of 73%, 66%, and 44%. Triple-validity rates are reported as 98%, 0%, and 55% for KGGen, GraphRAG, and OpenIE. Tables 2–4 add de-duplication, runtime, and cost outcomes; these are additional evaluations, not demonstrated same-setting gains over v1.

T1.justification: Neither version presents formal theoretical results, proofs, or derivations. v2's new procedures and descriptive evaluation ratios do not introduce a substantive mathematical theory.

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes superior extraction performance and an approximately 18% benchmark advantage. v2's abstract distinguishes comparable downstream retrieval from better information retention, while its contribution list introduces two benchmark tasks and improved scaling as central contributions. This materially changes the scope and emphasis of the headline claims.

C2.justification: v2 distinguishes downstream answer quality from conformity to traditional KG structure and attributes scaling benefits to de-duplication and relation reuse. It newly acknowledges possible LLM-judge bias and domain-specific limitations in medicine and finance. The corpus-size limitation changes from short texts to evaluation up to 5M tokens, still below the proposed web-scale application.

D1.justification: v2 supplies resolution parameters such as 128-item groups and 16 retrieved candidates, revised extraction/resolution prompts, and new RAG answering and judging prompts. Table 3 adds per-stage token usage, runtime, throughput, and cost, while the checklist adds laptop/API resource guidance. Both versions retain the same project repository reference.

R1.justification: Most extraction and KG-evaluation literature is retained. v2 adds the WikiQA citation and removes several references accompanying the shortened introduction, including Edge et al., Luo et al., and Pujara et al. It also revises the GraphRAG description to distinguish graph nodes and relationships from community summaries. The broader literature positioning remains recognizable.

P1.justification: The introduction is substantially rewritten, Related Work moves from Section 7 to Section 2, and method and benchmark explanations are reorganized. Appendix prompts are consolidated, the redundant validation appendix is removed, and the retained MINE prompts and example article are renumbered. A broader-impact section and NeurIPS checklist are added.

P2.justification: v2 adds the MINE-2 bar chart, four numbered tables, and Appendix D's scaling plot, substantially expanding the presentation of evidence. Existing figure images are retained and resized or relocated; v1 Figure 5 becomes v2 Figure 6. Typography, headings, prompt-box layout, and the title page are reformatted for the NeurIPS template.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's reliance on short synthetic texts and unvalidated LLM judging through downstream Wikipedia retrieval, human-annotated entity evaluation, and manual checks of judgments and triples. Resource measurements and more specific limitations also improve practical assessment. These gains are tempered by reporting inconsistencies: Figure 1 still depicts the old procedure, Figure 5 leaves error bars undefined, and GraphRAG's 1M-character runtime is 2,079.17 seconds in Table 4 but 2,319 seconds in Section 6.6. These weaknesses limit particular claims without outweighing the broader validation gains.
